## Summarising papers, writing, bullet point introductions

In this session, we cover summarising papers as well as general writing advice before specifically covering bullet point introductions. I then ask students to bring a bullet point introduction with them into the Semester 1 Week 7 session.

I've made some [notes for this session](https://github.com/AshleyERobertson/group_supervision/releases/download/resources-v1/Sem1Wk5_Resources1_2_3_Writing_and_Editing.docx). Feel free to use/adapt etc. as you wish.

### Expected progress

-   By now, I would be expecting to see some ethics drafts coming in and all projects should be firmed up. Rationales should all be submitted.

### Summarising papers

-   I cover some suggestions that I have on how to summarise papers
    -   Summarise with intent (what is the purpose?)
    -   Pull out the key details (remember can go back for further detail)
    -   Take notes for the Discussion, even when reading for the Introduction

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What I discuss with students: Summarising Papers

**Reading and note-taking**

-   Identify what the key points/findings/arguments are
-   Remember to avoid closely paraphrasing the original -- when taking notes, try to think about how you would summarise it for someone who has never read the paper.

**Judgement calls (weight and evaluation)**

-   Try to avoid summarising every single detail, as then it can become too lengthy. Remember that you can refer back to the paper if you need to.

    -   Have a focus for the summary -- what is your purpose?

    -   Help build a rationale?

    -   As background in the intro?

    -   Linking to theory?

    -   To link to findings in the Discussion?

-   Go beyond description and evaluate. What is great about the study? What is not-so-great? Why? What does this mean for how we interpret the study? How confident can we be with a study's conclusions?

-   Some papers will be more relevant (and therefore will have a longer summary) than others. If a paper seems great in terms of topic, it's not necessarily important to include in great detail if it's methodologically weak.

**Working across papers**

-   Once you've summarised a few papers, take a step back and consider how they relate to each other.
-   Look at where they agree/disagree/build on each other. When you write your dissertation, then keep this in mind: you want to think of the 'bigger picture' and synthesise, rather than producing study 1 -\> study 2 -\> study 3 -\> conclusion.

**Reading while being aware of later sections**

-   Even when reading papers in preparation for the introduction, keep an eye out for anything that might be useful for your Discussion.
-   I keep a document specifically for the Discussion and take notes from my reading as I go. I don't use all of these at the end, but it means I have some thoughts written down and don't have a blank space (which can be a bit overwhelming).
:::

### General writing advice

-   Writing advice will likely differ from supervisor to supervisor. Here are some of my suggestions (rest are in the document linked previously):
    -   It's better to write something than nothing
    -   Know what works for you (e.g. timing, accountability, blocking time out)
    -   Small goals can be helpful
    -   Split out **generation** and **editing**
        -   This can help get over the hurdle of the 'perfect' sentence

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What I discuss with students: Writing Advice

-   It's better to write something/anything than nothing.

    -   Be accountable to others

    -   Body doubling can be useful

    -   Block out time in your calendar

-   Give yourself small goals, e.g. ten minutes of writing.

    -   It makes it easier to get started. If I was really struggling, I would write down what I was struggling with. Sometimes, just typing something was enough to get me into it, even if I'd spent the first five mins writing 'I don't have a clue what to write about'

-   If writing feels like the wrong tool that day, try talking it through instead -- to a supervisor, a friend, or just to yourself. Saying it out loud can help you identify the structure of an argument faster than staring at a blank page

-   Know yourself (do you write better in the morning or at night?)

    -   I am better at creative things in the morning, so during my PhD I used to write every morning from 9-1, then the afternoon was spent doing things that didn't need my brain as much. Within the schedule you have, think about what might work for you

-   Writing out of order

    -   You don't have to write in the order it'll be read in -- if you're stuck on the intro, try starting with a different section (e.g. Methods) that feels more concrete. Getting words down anywhere builds momentum to go back to the harder sections later

-   I used to get hung up on every single sentence. What helped me was splitting the process of generation and editing

    -   Generation - just focus on getting words on a page. Don't worry about spelling, looking papers up, grammar, punctuation, structure etc. It's about getting the ideas down.

    -   Editing - later (give yourself some time between this stage and the generation stage), focus on getting the things you wrote into a coherent draft.

    -   To do this, try to split it into two stages:

        -   first, check the structure (does the argument hold together, is anything in the wrong place or missing),

        -   then focus on the line-level parts (grammar, word choice, polishing sentences). This then means you only polish those parts that seem likely to 'stick around' and make it past the first round of editing.
:::

### Bullet point introductions

-   I discuss that I would like everyone to write a bullet point introduction for the next session. I tell students that I do not expect this to be perfect, and that it can change down the line
-   We go through some of the suggestions I have for writing this.
-   I ask students to post on the Teams channel before the next group meeting (in two weeks time) but others may choose a different process
-   I signpost them to [Wil Toivo's resource](https://github.com/AshleyERobertson/group_supervision/releases/download/resources-v1/Sem1Wk5_Resource4_WilToivo_DevRationale.docx) on developing a rationale for their introduction.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What I discuss with students: Bullet Point Introductions

-   Set the scene for the reader
-   Do the different paragraphs flow well?
-   A good structure starts off broad and ends narrow (i.e. closer to your study)
-   It can be helpful to use sub-headings, especially if you are covering literature from quite different areas
-   Try to synthesise literature (i.e. pull together literature from various sources, rather than concentrate on a study per paragraph)
-   Be selective about which literature makes the cut, not just how much detail each gets (i.e. not everything that is interesting needs to be in the intro)
-   Is there a theoretical basis for your research?
-   Identify the gap -- what's missing, unresolved, or contested in the literature -- but remember to think about why it matters. "No one's studied this" isn't a justification on its own; ground the "why" in what's already known or unresolved, not in what the findings might lead to (save future implications for the Discussion)
-   Try drafting your RQ/hypotheses first, even roughly -- then check each bullet point is actually building towards it, rather than just being interesting background
-   End your introduction by presenting your RQ (qual) or your hypotheses (quant)
:::
